explanations.explanation: It detects when the text switches into a formal, symbol‐ and structure–rich register—that is, content written in specialized notations (mathematical formulas, scientific descriptions, embedded code, etc.) rather than plain everyday language. This feature activates on segments heavy with equations, technical symbols, and formal formatting that indicate domain‐specific, rigorously structured discussion.

This feature appears to signal when the model is processing formulaic or templated language – the kind of boilerplate text that shows up in user interface instructions, legal disclaimers, registration forms, and other standardized, structured content. In other words, it activates on fragments that use conventional “enter,” “of,” “terms,” copyright/license boilerplate, and similar interface text rather than free‐form narrative.

It appears that this feature “lights up” on tokens that mark structured, technical, or formal content—such as code identifiers, filenames, dates, mathematical symbols/formulas, and other domain‐specific constants—which tend to behave like fixed or syntactically salient elements distinct from the surrounding free‐form text.

It appears that this neuron “lights up” when the model is processing tokens that mark a structural or formatting boundary—in other words, words or fragments that serve as signposts between different text‐modes (for example, section headers, navigational or “read more” prompts, code/command snippets, or other meta‐information in mixed-format content). This feature seems to capture the abstract signal that a transition is occurring from one type of text (or content “zone”) to another.

It appears this feature “lights up” on text that directly addresses the reader—in other words, it detects a second‐person, interactive tone (with pronouns like “you” and accompanying directives and instructions) that is common in user interface messages, website help texts, and other direct, personalized communications.

It appears that this feature “lights up” when the model is processing structured, compound expressions – especially when a punctuation element (often a hyphen or a similar joining marker) is linking parts of a multi‐token proper name, technical term, or identifier. In other words, the feature seems to signal boundary or joining cues in compound or formally formatted text (such as hyphenated names, codes, patent numbers, or other complex identifiers) that require special treatment or integration in the model’s representation.

This feature consistently detects and marks the hyphenated connections within compound modifiers—phrases like “moderate‐to‐severe,” “proof‐of‐concept,” “24‐year‐old,” “state‐owned,” and similar constructions—indicating that it’s sensitive to the structure and semantic emphasis provided by hyphenation across varied contexts.

It is a detector for formal, structured language—identifying and “highlighting” embedded technical expressions (such as mathematical formulas in LaTeX, algorithmic pseudocode, SQL queries, and code snippets) by recognizing their characteristic syntax and semantic cues.

It zeroes in on subword “chunks”–the initial morpheme fragments that cut off longer, often compound or stylistically marked words in informal or click‐bait language. In other words, the feature consistently lights up on the beginnings of words (such as “Dis–” in “Disasters,” “Qu–” in “Quote” or “Quiz,” “j–” in “joker,” etc.) that are split off during tokenization, suggesting that these leading segments carry a particular semantic or stylistic weight in these varied, often sensational or creative texts.

It appears that the feature is picking up on code “import” or dependency‐declaration fragments—snippets where the syntax and tokens signal inclusion of external libraries or modules (whether in HTML linking to JS, C# “using” statements, package names in setup files, or similar).

It appears that the feature “fires” on text formatted like U.S. legal header material—that is, the boilerplate and structured case‐citation language found in appellate opinions (including court names, circuit identifiers, docket numbers, case parties, and filing/decision metadata).

It appears that this feature is “aware” of evaluative or judgment–marking language. In multiple contexts—from product descriptions and reviews to technical details and event summaries—it spikes on words or phrases that cue the reader into assessments, measurements, or qualifiers (for example, “seems,” “favorites,” “lots,” “terms,” “note,” “ensure,” “something to prove”). In short, the feature seems to pick out when the text is shifting to a subjective evaluation or comparison, flagging content that expresses or supports a judgment about quality, performance, or importance.

It “fires” on formulaic, boilerplate segments—text that follows a fixed, legal/administrative template such as copyright/license notices and standardized disclaimer language (or similarly rigid, structured instructions like time‐arithmetic questions).

It appears that this feature fires when the model is processing formal, structured citation or metadata strings—that is, passages containing the sort of all‐caps abbreviations, numbers, punctuation, and formatting markers (e.g. “WO … OD”, case and patent numbers, legal citations, publication headers) that one finds in legal, technical, or academic documents.

It identifies contexts where a program or expression is “pointing to” or extracting particular elements by means of identifiers and indexes—situations involving precise data‐referencing, ordering, or conversion of structured content (such as JSON, arrays, or table rows) for update, query, or mathematical processing.

This feature activates when the model encounters formally structured, boilerplate‐style text—that is, passages with rigid, domain‐specific syntax (such as SQL schema definitions, legal citations, HTML/markup headers, or code comments) that adhere to standardized formatting conventions.

It appears that the feature “lights up” on the connective, transition‐style words—especially tokens like “and” (often marked with near‐maximal activations) that occur in passages prompting the reader toward a next step or action. In other words, the feature is sensitive to the linguistic “call‐to‐action” or bridging conjunctions common in marketing copy, interactive instructions, or transition segments in online content.

It appears this feature “lights up” when the model encounters the distinctive, often alphanumerically‐mixed “head” of a multi–token identifier—that is, the central, properly capitalized (or stylized) element within product names, technical labels, or branded proper nouns. In other words, the feature detects the signature parts of compound names (whether software titles, model codes, or specific acronyms) that signal a domain‐specific identifier or technical term.
This feature activates when the text is introducing examples or illustrations—typically marked by phrases like “such as”—to clarify or expand on a preceding idea or category.

This feature appears to mark tokens that serve as the key “name‐carries” in formal or branded entities—parts of proper names, titles, or identifiers that distinguish places, products, events, or components (including in code or URLs). In effect, the feature is sensitive to the salient, typically capitalized or specially formatted, segments of multi–token names that cue the model to treat them as important, identity‐defining pieces in a wider context.
